automation_evidence.finding: Among the 36 largest U.S. audit firms (310,000+ resumes, 2010-2019), a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's share of AI workers predicted a 5.0% lower likelihood of a restatement, 1.4% lower likelihood of a material restatement, and a 0.3% lower likelihood of a restatement-related SEC investigation; audit fees fell 0.9%, 1.5% and 2.1% over the following one, two and three years, and total accounting headcount fell 3.6% after three years and 7.1% after four (junior-level staff down 5.7% and 11.8%).

Panel survey of 277 accountants plus field data from 79 small and mid-sized firms (hundreds of thousands of transactions) using an AI-based accounting platform: 55% increase in weekly client support volume, about 8.5% of accountant time reallocated from routine data entry to higher-value work, 12% increase in general ledger granularity, and a 7.5-day reduction in monthly close time. Experienced accountants intervened more when the tool's confidence scores signalled uncertainty.

Staggered rollout of a generative-AI assistant to 5,179 customer-support agents raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average, with a 34% gain for novice/low-skilled workers and minimal effect for experienced workers; customer sentiment and employee retention also improved. Adjacent task-type evidence (structured knowledge work with document/response drafting), not accounting-specific.

Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (Oct 23-Nov 5, 2023): 3.9% of U.S. businesses used AI to produce goods or services; Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services (the sector containing accounting firms) reported 9.1%, versus 13.8% in Information. Measures adoption, not time saved, and predates most firm-level generative-AI deployment.

A 150-person regional CPA firm (Cleveland, OH) reports a 30-60% reduction in associate time spent on audit evidence review after OCR-plus-LLM deployment in Q4 2024, against a baseline of roughly 1,900 hours per associate per year (1-15 minutes per control across 75-300 controls and 20-50 engagements). Single-firm self-report, no control group.

Vendor case study: HLB Mann Judd Perth reports 40-50% efficiencies on subsequent drafts of financial-statement reviews and about 600 hours saved annually across 300+ statement sets using AI review software.

Vendor case study: Johnson Lambert (insurance-sector audit) reports time per financial-risk audit falling from 60-80 hours to 12-16 hours after building a document-to-structure pipeline on Amazon Bedrock, with staff shifted from tie-outs to document review.

Self-commissioned survey (US and UK accounting/finance professionals) reports six in ten accountants still spend 40% or more of their time on manual work such as reconciliations, journal entries and transaction matching, and nearly one in five spend over 60%. Instrument and sampling are vendor-controlled.
Vendor survey of 300 UK accountants: 39% said they spend more than half of their day on manual tasks, while 30% said they lack tools to automate processes.

constraints: IRC Sec. 7216 makes it a misdemeanor for a return preparer to knowingly or recklessly disclose, or use for a purpose other than preparing a return, information furnished for return preparation: fine up to $1,000 ($100,000 where Sec. 6713(b) applies), up to 1 year imprisonment, or both (26 U.S.C. Sec. 7216, as amended 2019).

IRS Section 7216 regulations require taxpayer consent before return information is disclosed to or used by third parties, which constrains sending client tax data to external AI/cloud vendors without documented consent.

FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) explicitly lists tax preparation firms as 'financial institutions': a written information security program, encryption in transit and at rest, multi-factor authentication, service-provider oversight and contracts, annual reporting, and FTC breach notification within 30 days for incidents affecting 500+ consumers are required. This favours vetted, contracted AI vendors or private deployments.

Inference: audit and attest work is governed by documentation and independence standards (PCAOB/AICPA), so AI-generated conclusions must be traceable to cited source evidence and reviewed by a licensed professional; a practitioner account notes standards 'still apply in full' and that cited annotations strengthen the audit trail (source: Pease Bell article above).

Inference: because engagements involve client financial records and often personal tax data, data-residency, retention and deletion terms in vendor contracts are a gating design constraint for any agent handling client files; the FTC service-provider provisions make the firm responsible for the vendor's safeguards.
trends: Labor supply is contracting: accounting bachelor's and master's graduates fell to 55,152 in 2023-24, down 6.6% year over year, and new CPA Exam candidates fell from 42,626 (2023) to 28,082 (2024), even as 75% of hiring firms planned to hire the same number or more in 2025 (AICPA 2025 Trends, Oct 27, 2025).

BLS projects accountants and auditors to grow 5-6% over 2025-2035 with about 115,300 job openings, while bookkeeping/accounting/auditing clerks are projected to decline (-1% or lower) with about 144,100 openings from replacement demand (O*NET occupation summaries citing BLS 2025 wage and 2025-2035 projection data).

New Jersey industry scale (QCEW 2024, NAICS 5412 Accounting, Tax Preparation, Bookkeeping and Payroll Services, private ownership): 4,396 establishments and 42,391 employees, average annual pay $134,841, employment down 376 (-0.9%) and establishments down 55 (-1.2%) year over year.

Middlesex County (QCEW 2024, NAICS 5412, private): 346 establishments and 5,080 employees, average annual pay $149,231, employment roughly flat (-7 jobs, -0.1%) while establishments grew by 4 (+1.2%) - a dense, high-wage accounting cluster relative to the state.

Seasonality is structural: 55% of tax preparers report seasonal work schedules and 38% face time pressure every day (O*NET Work Context for SOC 13-2082), concentrating workload into the January-April filing window.

Work is repetitive and accuracy-critical by design: 68% of bookkeeping clerks and 41% of accountants rate repeating the same tasks as 'extremely important', and 81% / 69% respectively rate exactness as 'extremely important' (O*NET Work Context), which is what makes review-and-tie-out work both automatable and high-risk.
caveats: Wage figures are May 2025 BLS OEWS medians retrieved via the BLS public API (single-series queries); OEWS publishes New Jersey only at state level plus the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area, so Middlesex County is represented by the metro figure rather than a county estimate. QCEW 2024 figures are annual averages for private ownership in NAICS 5412 and are industry-wide averages that include partners' compensation effects, so they are not directly comparable to occupation medians. The strongest automation evidence (Fedyk et al.) measures AI hiring in the 36 largest audit firms from 2010-2019 - large-firm, pre-generative-AI, and about audit rather than tax or bookkeeping - so effect sizes should not be transferred to a 5-50 person local practice without adjustment. The Stanford working paper is not yet peer-reviewed and its field data come from one AI-software vendor's small and mid-sized firm clients, which likely over-represents adopters. Census BTOS measures self-reported AI use, not outcomes. Four of the nine evidence items are vendor or single-firm self-reports with no control group and are rated Low. No NJ- or Middlesex-specific measured automation study was found.
data_gaps: No OEWS estimates are published for an Edison/New Brunswick metro area; BLS's OEWS area list shows only Atlantic City-Hammonton, Trenton-Princeton and Vineland for New Jersey, so county-level wage data for Middlesex is unavailable (verified against https://download.bls.gov/pub/time-series/oe/oe.area).
No peer-reviewed or government study measuring AI time savings specifically in New Jersey accounting or bookkeeping firms was found.

ecfr.gov blocked automated access (CAPTCHA) when opening 26 CFR 301.7216, so consent requirements are described from the IRS Section 7216 information center and the statute rather than the regulation text itself.
